name: Liam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at Ridgeway Burgers, a sit-down burger franchise off the ring road that does about four hundred covers on a match day. I'm on the broiler and the build station, putting burgers together to spec, eight at a time. The franchise owner, Mr Kowalski, has already put in a fry robot, an arm that drops and lifts the baskets. I'm the junior on the line, and honestly my builds are still sloppier than they should be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the system, everything timed, everything measured, and I like that fry robot more than most people do. The match-day rush wears me out, and the noise. I use AI every day, to study the franchise manuals, to plan my budget, even to coach the under-twelves football team I help with. I live with my girlfriend Hannah, who's a dental receptionist, and we've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted it out, like it always does. The useful bits stay, the hype goes. Our fry robot stays, because it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd hoped to be the guy who understands the kitchen tech as it grew. But my job's fine, Ridgeway is busy and Hannah's is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, get my builds clean so Mr Kowalski moves me up to shift lead within a year. Keep saving, maybe start looking at what it costs to buy into a franchise one day. Keep using the AI tools for the manuals and the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, wanting more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into a franchise. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Serious, long term. It's a lot of money, more than we've got by a mile. But I'd rather own a franchise than work in one my whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about your money that worries you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Rent's fair, four months saved, Hannah and I split everything. The only thing is the football club, I keep paying for kit out of my own pocket.

say: The **market** sorted it out, like it always does: the useful bits stay and the hype goes.
Our **fry robot** stays, because it actually works.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, having hoped to grow with the **kitchen tech**.
My job is **fine**, with the restaurant busy and my girlfriend's work steady.
do: Clean up my **builds** to reach shift lead within a year.
Look into the cost of **buying a franchise**.
Keep using **AI tools** for manuals and coaching.
S0.quote: I'd rather own a franchise than work in one my whole life.
fieldNote: Liam already works beside a **fry robot** and likes it.
His money feels **secure**, and his drive is toward **ownership**.
He'd be **let down** by a plateau, wanting the tech to grow.

steps.text: Tidy his burger builds to win shift lead within a year
Keep using AI to study the franchise manuals
Price up what it costs to buy into a franchise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for people who are willing to learn. Businesses will get more efficient, and the workers who keep up will do fine. I'd say it to the lads at football too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my chance. Mr Kowalski will put in more machines, a robot broiler maybe. Someone has to run the new machines, and if that's me, I'm moving up, not out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Kowalski to send me on the franchise's equipment training this year. I'd learn the ordering and stock software the head office brings in. I'd keep saving toward the franchise, maybe put some into shares too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the cooks who don't want to learn the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Gary, who's been on the line eight years and hates the fry robot. I'd help him, I like Gary. But I don't think the business owes anyone a job if they won't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that how you'd want to be treated if it went the other way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'd want a chance to learn, that's all. Which is what I'd give Gary too.

say: This is good for people **willing to learn**.
Businesses get more **efficient**, and workers who **keep up** do fine.
think: This is **my chance**, because someone has to run the **new machines**.
If that's me, I'm **moving up**, not out.
do: Ask the owner for the franchise's **equipment training** this year.
Put some savings into **shares** alongside the franchise fund.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, like a door opening.
S1.quote: Someone has to run the new machines, and if that's me, I'm moving up, not out.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as a **promotion route**, not a threat.
His **free-market** view is softened by personal loyalty to an older colleague.
He holds himself to the same rule: a **fair chance** to learn.

steps.text: Go on the franchise's kitchen equipment training this year
Learn the head office ordering and stock software
Put part of his savings into shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so adapt, don't whine. I'd still say that. But I'd also say businesses should train their own people first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, 2028 means head office runs on AI, and by 2031 there's a robot that can build burgers better than me. Even the guy running the machines might not be needed for long. I'd be thirty-two, and the franchise dream might not make sense anymore if robots run it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on every equipment course going now, and aim to be the franchise's area technician by 2030, fixing robots across several sites. I'd save harder, six months. Hannah's front desk job goes to AI in 2028, so we'd plan for one income for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my skills, for the timing. Two years is tight even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hannah's job goes in 2028. What would you two do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably retrain as a dental nurse, that's hands-on, so she'd get a few more years. We'd tighten up. I'd stop paying for the football kit myself, sadly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to own a franchise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fully robot one, if the numbers work. Owning the robots might be the only safe job left. I don't know if I'd ever afford it though.

say: AGI is happening either way, so **adapt** and don't whine about it.
Businesses should still **train their own** people first, and I would say that out loud.
think: **Robots by 2031** could build burgers better than me.
Even **running the machines** might not last, and the franchise **dream** could fade.
do: Take every **equipment course** going, starting now.
Aim to become an **area technician** fixing robots by 2030.
Plan to live on **one income** while my girlfriend retrains.
S2.quote: Owning the robots might be the only safe job left.
fieldNote: Even an adaptive believer in markets finds **two years tight**.
His partner's **front-desk job** is exposed in 2028, before his.
He shifts from **ownership** dreams to repair work as the safer bet.

steps.text: Sign up for every franchise equipment course this year
Apply to be the franchise's area robot technician by 2030
Save six months of household money
Stop paying for the football club's kit himself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone who's serious. I'd be telling the younger lads at Ridgeway to get skilled up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, 2031 for AGI, 2034 for robots, I'd be thirty-five. That's time to become the technician and maybe buy a small share in a franchise before it all changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Equipment training this year, shift lead next year, area technician by 2030. Save and maybe go in with Mr Kowalski on a second site around 2032, if he'll have me. Hannah retrains early, while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in a good way. Busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Going in with Mr Kowalski. Has he ever hinted at that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, after a match day, he said I've got an owner's head. That's all. But I remember it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger lads, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn how the fry robot works, don't just stand next to it. Read the manual, ask the engineer questions when he comes. That's free training.

say: **Five years** is enough for anyone who's **serious**.
I'd tell the younger cooks at Ridgeway to **get skilled up**.
think: Robots arrive around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
There's time to become the **technician** and maybe buy a **franchise share**.
do: Reach **area technician** by 2030 via training and shift lead.
Offer to **co-invest** in a second site with the owner around 2032.
Help my girlfriend **retrain early**, while there's time.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mostly in a **good, busy** way.
S3.quote: Learn how the fry robot works, don't just stand next to it.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan into a clear **ladder** toward part-ownership.
He treats the visiting **engineer** as free training.
His **partner's** retraining is planned early, not forced.

steps.text: Work up to area technician by 2030
Offer to co-invest with the owner in a second restaurant
Help his girlfriend train as a dental nurse early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who doesn't use it only has themselves to blame. Maybe that's harsh. I'd say it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd love this one. Ten years to build up savings and skills, then robots around 2039 when I'm forty and hopefully owning a site. I'd buy the robots myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shift lead, then technician, then franchisee by about 2034. Marry Hannah, have kids. Keep coaching the football and teach the kids how the machines work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it might be harsh. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, again, and people like him. Ten years is plenty, but some people just won't. I'd still give him a job at my site if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own kids to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where they own something, a business, a trade. Not just hours for wages. Whatever the robots do, owners still get a say.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and not using it is your own **fault**.
Maybe that's **harsh**, but I'd say it anyway.
think: Robots around **2039** could find me **owning a site**.
I'd be the one **buying the robots** myself, instead of losing my job to them.
do: Rise to **franchisee** by about 2034 via shift lead and technician.
Keep **coaching** the under-twelves and teach them about machines.
S4.quote: Whatever the robots do, owners still get a say.
fieldNote: With a decade, he sees **ownership** as fully within reach.
His tough line softens into **loyalty** to an older colleague.
He wants his children to **own** something, not just sell hours.

steps.text: Buy into a Ridgeway franchise by about 2034
Marry his girlfriend and start a family
Keep coaching the under-twelves football team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hannah's job goes first and mine soon after, and two years isn't enough even if you're keen. What would help is franchises training their own cooks to run and fix the robots, and small business loans for people who want to buy in. Not handouts, a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who's going to own the robots. If it's only big companies, people like me are stuck. If a cook can save up and buy a robot, that's a different world.

headlineQuote: If a cook can save up and buy a robot, that's a different world.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old line cook** at a busy burger franchise that already uses a fry **robot**.
He lives with his girlfriend, a **dental receptionist**, and they have about four months saved.
He's **traditional** and pro-market, coaches kids' football and uses **AI every day**.
He sees robots as a **ladder** toward technician work and owning a **franchise**.
He stays **calm** in most scenarios but turns **anxious** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when his girlfriend's job goes first and two years is too **tight** to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: Franchises **training cooks** to run robots, and **small loans** to buy in.
